cases.question: Why was March 2018 so bad for deliveries?
cases.headline: March 2018 saw a sharp rise in late deliveries, with 19.0% of orders late compared to a 5.8% baseline, driven mainly by longer transit times.
notes: Late rate reached 19.0% in March 2018, up 13.2 percentage points from the 5.8% baseline.
Transit time averaged 12.97 days, about 3.9 days longer than the 9.06-day baseline, while handling time was nearly unchanged (3.33 vs 3.19 days).
The increase was systemic, with elevated late rates across states and categories; RJ had the highest excess late orders (208), followed by SP (158) and MG (147).
Late deliveries were associated with much lower customer satisfaction: average review score 2.07 vs 4.21 for on-time orders, and 59.3% one-star reviews vs 7.9%.
Top sellers contributed only 11.5% of late orders, indicating the issue was not concentrated in a few sellers.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Some category samples are small (e.g., audio with 33 orders), so rates may be unstable.

cases.question: Why were deliveries to Rio de Janeiro so late in March 2018?
cases.headline: Deliveries to Rio de Janeiro in March 2018 were unusually late: 34.5% of orders arrived late, compared with a baseline of 10.5%.
notes: The late rate was 34.5%, 24 percentage points above the baseline of 10.5%.
Transit time averaged 21.08 days, about 9.7 days longer than the baseline of 11.35 days.
Handling time was 3.21 days, slightly below the baseline of 3.28 days.
The delay was concentrated in categories such as garden tools (46.9% late), watches and gifts (45.8%), and bed, bath and table (41.7%).
Late orders received much lower review scores (average 1.67) than on-time orders (4.06), with 72.6% of late orders rated one star.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
The analysis is based on 864 delivered orders, of which 298 were late; some category samples are small (e.g., 32 garden tools orders).

cases.question: Why did review scores drop in March 2018?
cases.headline: Review scores in March 2018 were below the baseline, with an average of 3.75 versus 4.11, and the drop was concentrated in one-star reviews associated with late delivery.
notes: Average review score fell to 3.75 from a baseline of 4.11, a decline of 0.36 points.
One-star reviews rose to 19.0% of all reviews, compared with 10.9% at baseline, an increase of 8.1 percentage points.
Among one-star reviews, 56.6% were associated with late delivery, versus 33.0% for on-time delivery and 10.4% for not delivered.
Late delivery contributed 7.8 points to the one-star share increase, while on-time contributed 0.3 points and not delivered had no net effect.
The categories with the largest score declines were audio (2.94 vs 3.92), construction tools (3.36 vs 4.11), and toys (3.63 vs 4.19).
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Some category and seller samples are small (e.g., audio had 33 reviews), so their averages may be less stable.
Seller-level attribution can be affected by multiple sellers fulfilling the same product.

cases.question: Why were deliveries so bad in July 2017?
cases.headline: July 2017 was not unusual for late deliveries compared with the baseline; the late rate was 2.8%, which is 4.2 percentage points lower than the baseline of 7.0%.
notes: The late delivery rate in July 2017 was 2.8%, compared with a baseline of 7.0%, a decrease of 4.2 percentage points.
Handling time was 3.11 days versus 3.21 days baseline, and transit time was 8.51 days versus 9.38 days baseline, both slightly faster.
Promised delivery time was 23.32 days versus 23.66 days baseline, essentially unchanged.
No state showed an increase in late orders; the top three states by volume (SC, PR, RS) all had lower late rates than baseline.
Some categories had higher late rates than baseline (e.g., consoles_games at 11.1% vs 5.9%), but volumes were small and did not affect the overall rate.
caveats: The data shows where delay occurred, not why (observational data).
Order-level lateness is attributed to every seller in a multi-seller order.
Category-level analysis is based on small sample sizes (e.g., 45 orders for consoles_games).
Seller-level analysis shows one seller with a higher late rate (7.8% vs 1.7% baseline) but only 51 orders, so the impact is limited.

cases.question: Why did revenue fall in June 2018?
cases.headline: June 2018 was not unusual compared with the baseline: the average review score was 4.28, slightly above the baseline of 4.08, and the share of one-star reviews was lower (7.9% vs 11.7%).
notes: The average review score in June 2018 was 4.28, which is 0.20 points higher than the baseline of 4.08.
One-star reviews made up 7.9% of reviews, compared with 11.7% in the baseline, a decrease of 3.8 percentage points.
Among one-star reviews, 82.0% were associated with on-time delivery, 7.7% with late delivery, and 10.4% with not delivered.
The categories with the lowest average scores were small appliances (3.9), housewares (3.94), and drinks (4.0), all close to their baselines.
The top driver was none, indicating no single factor stood out.
caveats: Review scores are associations with delivery outcomes, not proof of cause.
Each order counts once, with its latest answered review; review text is not used.
Some category and seller samples are small (e.g., 30-43 reviews), so their averages may be less reliable.
Seller-level attribution may be affected by multiple sellers fulfilling orders.
